scenario_stem:
Cinderhill Deli Foods is a private limited company in Country X preparing chilled ready meals in a single kitchen opened 5 years ago. Founder Dana Whitmore employs 16 chefs and packers, and last year revenue was $1.05 million from selling 2,400 trays a day to local shops across two districts. Each worker currently performs every stage, from preparing and cooking to chilling and sealing.

Dana is deciding whether to reorganise the kitchen into a division-of-labour line with 4 specialist stations, needing 2 new vacuum-sealing machines at $9,600 each, or to keep the flexible all-round method. Specialists would lift output to 3,400 trays a day, but training each chef on all 4 stages takes 9 days under the current system, and the shops above all want reliable repeat orders.

questions.question_text: Define 'division of labour'.
questions.model_answer: Division of labour is when the production process is split into separate tasks and each worker is assigned one specific task or a small group of related tasks. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Production process is split into separate tasks/stages
Each worker concentrates on one/a few tasks

questions.model_answer: Factor 1: Labour is the human effort used in production [k]; Cinderhill employs 16 chefs and packers to prepare, cook, chill and seal each tray of meals [app]. Factor 2: Capital refers to man-made resources used to produce goods [k]; the 2 new vacuum-sealing machines at $9,600 each would add machinery to the kitchen [app].

knowledge_max_2: Labour is the human input/effort used in production
Capital is man-made resources such as machinery used to produce goods
application_max_2: 16 chefs and packers prepare, cook, chill and seal the meals
Vacuum-sealing machines are capital equipment bought/used for the kitchen

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of division of labour for Cinderhill Deli Foods.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Division of labour allows workers to specialise in one task, increasing speed and skill [k]; Cinderhill could lift output from 2,400 to 3,400 trays a day with its 4 specialist stations [app], which raises productivity so more meals are sold without hiring extra chefs [an]. Benefit 2: Repeating the same task helps workers make fewer errors [k]; specialist sealing-station staff would produce fewer rejected trays [app], reducing wasted ingredients and protecting the $1.05 million revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: Specialisation in a task increases skill and speed
Repetition reduces errors/wastage and raises productivity
application_max_2: Output rises from 2,400 to 3,400 trays a day with 4 specialist stations
Specialist staff at the sealing station make fewer rejected trays
analysis_max_2: Higher productivity means more meals sold without extra wage costs
Fewer rejects protect revenue and reduce waste costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Cinderhill Deli Foods should introduce the division-of-labour line? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One case for the line is productivity: splitting work into 4 specialist stations would lift output from 2,400 to 3,400 trays a day [k], an extra 1,000 trays daily for Cinderhill's local shop customers [app], spreading the $19,200 cost of the 2 vacuum-sealing machines over far more meals [an]. However, division of labour can make work monotonous and reduces flexibility [k]; Dana's chefs currently cover every stage, so the kitchen keeps running if one person is absent [app], meaning a rigid line could halt production when specialist staff are sick [an]. Overall, the case for the line is strong because demand is steady and the gain of 1,000 trays a day outweighs the cost [eval], but Dana should keep some chefs trained on all stages to protect flexibility [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Weighs up both options using stem figures (extra 1,000 trays vs $19,200 cost)
Reaches a justified recommendation with a sensible caveat

scenario_stem:
Brightneedle Garment Co is a private limited company in Country X manufacturing school uniforms at a purpose-built factory opened 7 years ago. Owner Ravi Menon employs 22 machinists and 3 cutters; last year it produced 900 shirts a week and revenue was $1.36 million. Each machinist currently sews whole shirts from start to finish and is paid the same time rate.

Ravi is deciding whether to introduce specialisation by stage: cutting, collar attachment, body assembly, finishing and quality checking, or keep whole-shirt sewing. The staged method would need 6 new overlocker machines at $3,200 each and could lift output to 1,150 shirts a week; whole-shirt sewing keeps machinists flexible but causes a 12% defect rate and frequent rework on collar seams.

questions.model_answer: Specialisation is when a worker, business or economy concentrates on producing a narrow range of products or carrying out a limited number of tasks. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Concentration on a narrow range of products/tasks
Can apply to a worker, business or country

questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Repetitive work can become boring and lower motivation [k]; Brightneedle's machinists would sew the same collar attachment all day instead of a whole shirt [app]. Problem 2: Over-specialisation reduces flexibility when a stage is short-staffed [k]; with only 3 cutters, an absence could leave 22 machinists waiting for cut pieces [app].

knowledge_max_2: Repetitive/monotonous work can lower motivation and morale
Over-specialisation reduces flexibility/interdependence between stages
application_max_2: Machinists would repeat one stage such as collar attachment daily

Benefit 2: A dedicated quality checker catches faults earlier [k]; a specialist checker could reduce the 12% defect rate [app], so fewer garments are reworked and less fabric is wasted [an].

Specialist quality checking catches faults earlier/raises quality

analysis_max_2: Higher output per machinist raises revenue without extra wage costs
Fewer defects reduce rework, saving fabric and labour time

questions.question_text: Do you think Brightneedle Garment Co should introduce specialisation by stage? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One case for specialisation is higher output and lower defects: the 5-stage system with 6 new overlockers at $3,200 each would lift production from 900 to 1,150 shirts a week [k], helping Brightneedle meet its shirt demand within its existing staffing [app], spreading the $19,200 machine cost across an extra 250 shirts weekly [an]. Conversely, specialisation may bore machinists and weaken the flexible whole-shirt method [k]; Ravi's team currently cover for each other, and repetitive collar work could increase costly rework [app], weakening quality if any single stage becomes a bottleneck [an]. Overall, the staged system is worth adopting because output and quality gains outweigh the monotony risk [eval], provided Ravi rotates tasks and monitors the defect rate weekly [eval].

scenario_stem:
Harvest Lane Print Co is a private limited company in Country X printing catalogues, labels and posters from a rented unit in a market town since 2019. Owner Priya Nair employs 12 print operators and 2 sales staff; last year revenue was $880,000 and net profit was $96,000. The business faces heavy price competition from an online rival undercutting it by 25% on most catalogue work.

Priya must choose between buying a $240,000 automated digital press that would run crewless overnight, or hiring 4 more operators at $21,000 a year each to expand capacity. The press would double output to 60,000 sheets a shift but makes 3 roles redundant; extra operators keep jobs but raise wage costs by $84,000 a year and need training time.

Factor 2: Enterprise is the risk-taking factor that organises the others [k]; owner Priya Nair organises the business and is deciding whether to invest in the new press [app].

Benefit 2: Consistent machine quality reduces errors [k]; overnight automated runs would reduce reprints on catalogue jobs [app], protecting the $96,000 profit from wasted paper and ink [an].

Automation gives consistent quality and fewer errors

questions.model_answer: One case for the press is competitiveness: at $240,000 it is costly, but doubling output to 60,000 sheets a shift lets Harvest Lane cut unit costs and match the online rival's 25% lower prices [k], protecting the $880,000 revenue produced by its 12 operators [app], and the crewless overnight run raises capacity without raising wage costs [an]. However, the press makes 3 roles redundant and removes jobs from a small market town [k]; losing experienced operators may also weaken customer service offered by the 2 sales staff [app], and redundancies could damage morale among remaining workers [an]. Overall, buying the press is the stronger option because it secures price competitiveness, and Priya could redeploy the 3 affected workers to finishing and delivery [eval]; the decision therefore protects both the business and most jobs [eval].

scenario_stem:
Olive Branch Kitchen Co is a private limited company in Country X preparing ready-to-cook meal kits from a unit near a wholesale market since 2021. Founder Marcus Vale employs 9 cooks and packers; last year it sold 52,000 kits at $12 each, giving revenue of $624,000. Each kit's ingredients cost $5.50, leaving $6.50 of added value per kit on every sale.

Marcus is deciding how to increase added value: either pre-chop ingredients and add recipe cards with more labour, or rebrand with premium packaging costing $0.85 extra per kit. The prep option would lift perceived quality but add 14 hours of labour a week; the rebrand targets busy professionals and could support a $2 price rise across the kit range.

questions.model_answer: Added value is the difference between the selling price of a product and the cost of the bought-in materials and components used to make it. [2]

Way 2: Convenient preparation saves customers time [k]; kits save busy buyers the effort of shopping and chopping across 52,000 kits a year [app].

Way 2: Better packaging and branding can raise the price customers will pay [k]; spending $0.85 extra per kit on premium packaging could support a $2 price rise [app], lifting added value per kit from $6.50 to $7.65 even after packaging costs [an].

However, the pre-chop alternative deepens real product value [k]; recipe cards and chopped ingredients make every kit genuinely more convenient for Marcus's customers [app], which could build loyalty and repeat orders rather than relying on looks alone [an]. scenario_stem:
Northbarrow Garment Works is a private limited company in Country X producing embroidered workwear and club uniforms from a factory in a rural town since 2016. Owner Sofia Lindqvist employs 14 sewers and 2 embroiderers; last year output was 30,000 garments and revenue was $1.8 million. Hand embroidery takes 5 days per 100 garments and every badge is stitched to order.

Sofia is deciding whether to buy 2 computerised embroidery machines at $18,500 each to replace the 2 hand embroiderers, or keep hand embroidery, which customers say is unique. The machines would cut embroidery time by 80% and allow the firm to accept a new 12,400-garment contract from a national supermarket chain, boosting monthly output significantly over the coming year.

Founder Owen Barrett employs 6 print operators and 1 apprentice; last year revenue was $310,000. Orders have risen 15% since a rival closed and both presses are fully booked most Saturdays across the whole working week.

Owen is considering launching a personalised wedding-stationery range to use spare capacity, costing $7,500 for design set-up and marketing. He would need to buy stock upfront and compete with several established stationery sellers serving local venues, but a 25% mark-up on kits could add $18,000 a year in profit if he wins the local wedding market from June onwards.

Difficulty 2: Competing against established stationery sellers is hard for a small local firm [k]; Alderline has no reputation in weddings compared with specialist sellers [app], so winning trust and enough sales to earn the expected $18,000 a year may take longer than planned [an].

Ambermill Foods Ltd is a private limited company in Country X preparing school lunches and retail salad bowls from a 9-year-old single kitchen. Founder Grace Okafor employs 10 staff; last year revenue was $580,000 from two main sales channels. Grace holds a school-lunch contract worth $320,000 a year, but her retail salad bowls sold 900 units a week at $4.50 through convenience shops.
